Treg Bernt, a Meridian Republican, on Thursday announced they plan to introduce a bill during the upcoming legislative session to require so-called e-motos — which […]
text:
Idaho Legislature may clamp down on high powered e-motorbikes amid injuries
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Two Idaho lawmakers from Ada County are teaming up to introduce a bill to regulate high powered e-motorbikes, citing an uptick injuries.
Rep. Brooke Green, a Boise Democrat, and Sen. Treg Bernt, a Meridian Republican, on Thursday announced they plan to introduce a bill during the upcoming legislative session to require so-called e-motos — which they say can reach over 30 mph but are often marketed as e-bikes — to be classified as motorcycles. That change would require riders of e-motos to have a driver’s license with a motorcycle endorsement to ride on public roads, and for the vehicles to meet certain requirements to be considered street legal, the lawmakers say.
Since the start of the year, Idaho emergency rooms have seen nearly 1,900 visits due to electric mobility devices, a category that also includes e-bikes and e-scooters, according to data from the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare. Young boys, between the ages of 11 and 15, accounted for 306 of the visits — the most of any demographic reported. An Idaho Statesman report published earlier Thursday highlighted the spike in injuries.
“Families are spending thousands of dollars on what they believe are bicycles, without realizing their 14-year-old cannot legally ride them down Eagle Road or on the Greenbelt,” Bernt and Green said in a joint statement. “Kids are getting seriously hurt, and we need to address this before more injuries occur.”
Ahead of the holiday season, the lawmakers urged parents to not buy e-motos for children who can’t legally drive motorcycles on public roads.
The proposed statewide change seems similar to an action the city of Boise took earlier this year.
Other cities have taken notice, too.
Meridian in July launched an education campaign focused on the use of e-bikes and e-motorcycles, BoiseDev reported. Nampa in September passed an ordinance adding local regulations, including barring e-motos from sidewalks and greenbelts if they can reach speeds in excess of 28 miles per hour, the Idaho Statesman reported.
“There’s nothing wrong with enjoying these vehicles in the desert or on our public lands where motorized recreation is permitted, but motorcycles do not belong on the Greenbelt, sidewalks, or other pedestrian spaces,” the lawmakers added. “We want parents to have the facts before making expensive holiday purchases, and we’re working on bipartisan legislation to establish clear rules that keep our communities safe.”

title: Mitch Wieland Reads “After a Rainstorm” by Robert Wrigley
summary: On the third week of November, Mitch Wieland reads “After a Rainstorm,” a poem by Robert Wrigley.
text:
Before her death in Auschwitz at the age of 29, Etty Hillesum experienced spiritual awakenings even in her darkest days. Hillesum was a writer and thinker, Dutch and Jewish, later known for her letters and journals about time under Nazi occupation in the Netherlands. Her work was finally collected and published in 1981 under the title “An Interrupted Life.” She wrote not of finding ecstasy in external things, but allowing life to happen and finding peace within.
“I know and share the many sorrows a human being can experience, but I do not cling to them,” she wrote. “They pass through me, like life itself, as a broad eternal stream.”
She’d witnessed her entire family’s disappearance - parents and two brothers - all at the hands of the Nazi regime, all later killed. Her final written words were a postcard dropped from a train, thanking those left behind in the ghetto for their “kindness and care.”
“Ultimately, we have just one moral duty,” she’d written the year before. “To reclaim large areas of peace in ourselves, more and more peace, and to reflect it toward others. And the more peace there is in us, the more peace there will also be in our troubled world.”
It’s the third week of November and we’re hearing writing along the theme of reclamation this month. Today, Mitch Wieland shares a poem by Robert Wrigley, titled “After a Rainstorm." A poet and educator with fellowships from the Guggenheim Foundation and the National Endowment for the Arts, Wrigley has published over 15 collections of poetry, including his most recent, “A True Account of Myself as a Bird.”
Something I Heard is supported by Idaho Commission on the Arts and the National Endowment for the Arts.

title: After feds let states delay Medicaid work requirements, Idaho officials unsure if they’ll take it
summary: Nearly a week after federal regulators let states delay Medicaid work requirements, Idaho health officials say they’re still deciding if they’ll take it. Last week, the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services extended the deadline for states to implement work requirements from Jan. 1 to June 30. The move came amid hurdles in several […]
text:
After feds let states delay Medicaid work requirements, Idaho officials unsure if they’ll take it
More than a fifth of Idahoans removed from Medicaid have since-re-enrolled, new data shows. (Getty Images)
Nearly a week after federal regulators let states delay Medicaid work requirements, Idaho health officials say they’re still deciding if they’ll take it.
Last week, the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services extended the deadline for states to implement work requirements from Jan. 1 to June 30. The move came amid hurdles in several states.
Idaho officials request raise for disability caregivers and restoring cuts to mental health services
A spokesperson for the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare on Wednesday said the agency is mulling its next steps.
“We just found this out on Friday and are still reviewing our options and readiness for further implementation,” agency spokesperson AJ McWhorter told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email.
The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare has been planning to implement the work requirements on Jan. 1. Under the federal “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” work requirements, also called community engagement requirements, require people enrolled in Medicaid expansion to prove that they are working, doing community service or educational or training activities for at least 80 hours each month.
About 82,500 Idahoans are enrolled in Medicaid expansion, the state says. Medicaid work requirements and other changes in the “Big Beautiful Bill” could kick 20,000 to 34,000 Idahoans off Medicaid expansion by 2028, according to an analysis by the Urban Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation.
But in July, state health officials said their initial review found that 68,400 Idahoans on Medicaid expansion met the new work requirements. About 63% of people on Medicaid expansion across the country are working, according to KFF, a health policy research group.
If Idaho doesn’t take the six-month delay for work requirements, it wouldn’t be the first federal leniency the state passed up on this policy. The state health agency said this summer that it wouldn’t give Medicaid expansion patients who have disabilities a one-year grace period to not provide proof that their condition interferes with their ability to comply with work requirements.

title: 17 new felonies added against Boise chiropractor accused of secretly recording women, children
summary: 17 new felonies added against Boise chiropractor accused of secretly recording women, children Idaho News 6
text:
BOISE, Idaho — Seventeen new felony charges have been added against Nathaniel Hearon, the Boise chiropractor accused of secretly recording women and children and possessing child sexual abuse material.
During a preliminary hearing Friday, prosecutors presented an amended complaint adding the 17 charges. Hearon previously faced 10 felony counts of possessing or accessing child sexually exploitative material.
RELATED | $2M bail remains for Boise chiropractor accused of secretly recording women, children
According to information presented in court Friday, the additional charges include 16 video-related counts and one additional child-exploitation-related count, bringing the total number of felony charges against Hearon to 27.
Hearon appeared for Friday's hearing via Zoom from the Ada County Jail.
Prosecutors previously said they expected to file additional charges as investigators continued reviewing evidence. Earlier in the investigation, Boise police said they had identified numerous local victims and alleged some recordings were made at Hearon's chiropractic workplace and other locations.
PREVIOUS COVERAGE | Boise man accused of recording women and girls at chiropractic clinic, police say
Hearon is expected to be arraigned on the new charges at his next court appearance, scheduled for Dec. 4 at 8:30 a.m.
Idaho News 6 will continue following the case.

title: Idaho Botanical Garden expansion aims to build community
summary: Earlier this year, the Idaho Botanical Garden nearly doubled in size at its picturesque location nestled at the base of the Boise Foothills.
text:
Earlier this year, the Idaho Botanical Garden nearly doubled in size at its picturesque location nestled at the base of the Boise Foothills.
The 10-acre expansion brings with it an arboretum in its infancy stage. The young trees will eventually grow to tower over visitors and offer much needed shade to the garden.
It also includes a new event lawn and several new gardens showcasing plants that heal us, amaze us or help feed us.
The staff even extended the new experience to the parking lot and new bike pavilion where happy succulents and cacti will poke out from crags in the wall to greet visitors.
James Dawson recently got a tour of the new spaces and brings us this postcard.
Editor's note: The Idaho Botanical Garden is a financial supporter of Boise State Public Radio, but had no involvement with the development or production of this story.
A transcript of the audio tour is available below:
Colin Lyman: So my name is Colin Lyman. I'm the director of horticulture and facilities at Idaho Botanical Garden. So I'm over everything outside: buildings, infrastructure and plants. So we are right below where our old entrance used to be. And we're standing in the the new bike garden. We can fit 177 to 200 bikes in here. There's lots of bike hoops. We have a raised planter beds with seat walls for seating, a bike pavilion, and then we have our rock wall. And in the wall there's little cracks and nooks and crannies that next spring we'll be installing cactus and succulents all the way throughout because there's so much concrete below it. We can the heat from that reflects, and we can create microclimates to grow things that normally wouldn't be able to grow.
Colin Lyman: Right next to the bike garden is the parking garden. We call it a parking garden, because the whole point of it is to be full of plant material, so that when you drive into the garden to park, you feel immersed in the experience when you arrive, and you can feel that, especially right now in the border bed that ligns Old Penitentiary Road. It's very full. Right now, we have some space empty. We're planning more things this fall. Because of the diversity of the plant list, some of the things were difficult to find. To the left of our kiosks is the future home of the Boise Farmers Market. Right now it's a gravel pad, but it's the future site of our events building, education building and an administration building. We looked at event space. title: Commentary: Idaho nonprofit Envision provides the gift of sight and hearing
summary: Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision, figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss. Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way. “I’ve […]
text:
Idaho nonprofit Envision provides the gift of sight and hearing
Envision offers free vision clinics for those at, or below, the poverty levels, and demand is high, writes guest columnist Chuck Malloy.
Idaho nonprofit Envision helps provide eye exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. (Photo by Getty Images)
Jay Lugo, the executive director of Envision, figures he’s had a good day if his nonprofit enterprise can help one person with vision or hearing loss.
Lugo has had a lot of good days during his 32 years leading the Lions Clubs-affiliated nonprofit, and he has seen thousands of Idahoans helped along the way.
“I’ve seen people break down and cry when they put on a pair of glasses and discover they are able to see,” Lugo says. “It fills my heart with joy being able to do that – and I sleep well at night knowing that we are making a difference. But it’s not just me. It’s the volunteers and office co-workers who see that happen, and the 1,400 Lions Club members throughout the state who get information about what’s being done. So, a lot of people are involved.”
And Lance Grady of Boise is glad for that. He didn’t break down in tears when he recently was fitted with glasses, but he did look across a street and see a squirrel climbing a tree. And he could see letters, numbers and names on buildings.
“I wouldn’t have been able to see any of that without my glasses,” he said. “This has been life changing. I can drive and do other things that I was unable to do.”
Grady’s story began by word of mouth.
“A family friend talked with me about reaching out to the Lions,” he said. “They were determined to help me find something – without spending $400 for a pair of glasses. “I’m so thankful … a lot of stress has been lifted from me.”
Lugo has seen similar stories play out many times.
“When people are able to see, they can get a driver’s license, fill out a job application and be productive,” Lugo says. “There is such a big gap with healthcare, and we’re only talking about eyesight and hearing. The state doesn’t provide aid with eyeglasses for those over the age of 18, so you are not going to get eyecare assistance if you are at the poverty level.”
Envision helps fill the void, providing exams, eyeglasses and frames for free or at discounted rates, depending on income levels. Envision offers free vision clinics for those at, or below, the poverty levels, and Lugo says demand is high.
“I get at least 20 applications in my email box every day, which is about 600 a month,” he says. “Every one of those are from people who need glasses and are at the poverty level. There are a lot of people who are hurting.”
Envision started in 1969 as Idaho’s only eye bank and arranging corneal transplants remain a big part of the nonprofit’s operation – along with the tradition of collecting and refurbishing used eyeglasses. title: Idaho Matters Doctor Roundtable: November 18, 2026
summary: For the first time in more than 25 years, the United States has lost its status as a country that has eliminated measles.
text:
For the first time in more than 25 years, the United States has lost its status as a country that has eliminated measles. It's a pretty stunning reversal for a disease that was once considered a public health success story.
More than 5,400 cases have been reported across 45 states this year and ten people have died. To put that in perspective, the U.S. averaged about 180 measles cases a year between 2000 and 2024.
Health experts say the outbreak is being fueled by falling vaccination rates. Just 92% of kindergartners are now vaccinated against measles, below the 95% generally needed to prevent outbreaks.
This is about more than measles. Public health experts warn that other diseases we've long been able to control through vaccination could also make a comeback.
How did we get here and what does this mean for the future of public health in this country?
Dr. David Pate, the former CEO of St. Luke's Health System and the author of the book "Preparing for the Next Global Outbreak," joined Idaho Matters to talk more about these topics and answer listener questions!
If you have public health questions, send us an email at idahomatters@boisestate.edu.

title: After state employees didn’t get raises in 2026, Idaho state legislator pay frozen for 1 year
summary: Idaho state legislator pay will be frozen in place at $25,000 for the next year, in line with state employees who did not get a pay increase from legislators this year. Then, starting Dec. 1, 2027, the annual base pay for legislators is set to increase by about 6.7%, up to $26,685. Members of the […]
text:
After state employees didn’t get raises in 2026, Idaho state legislator pay frozen for 1 year
Citizens committee holds pay flat at $25,000 this year, but in December 2027, pay will bump up to $26,685
House Speaker Mike Moyle, standing at right, speaks to the 2026 Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation on Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Clark Corbin/Idaho Capital Sun)
Idaho state legislator pay will be frozen in place at $25,000 for the next year, in line with state employees who did not get a pay increase from legislators this year.
Then, starting Dec. 1, 2027, the annual base pay for legislators is set to increase by about 6.7%, up to $26,685.
Members of the 2026 Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation voted 5-1 to approve holding legislative pay flat for one year and then increasing it next year.
House Speaker Mike Moyle, R-Star, had recommended increasing the base pay to $26,685 starting Dec. 1 of this year, but the committee held pay flat this year after committee members Tom Harris and Bryan Mooney pointed out that state employee pay was held flat this year.
“I have that in the back of my mind for the citizens and other state employees that didn’t get a raise, and I think it sends the right message if they didn’t get a raise,” Mooney said Thursday.
In addition to the base pay, an unstructured constituent services allowance all legislators receive will increase to a flat $6,000. Most legislators previously received $2,500 per year in constituent services allowance, although legislators who live in geographically large legislative districts received up to $5,300. Moving forward, there will be no distinction between district sizes.
Under the Idaho Constitution, state legislators do not have the power to set their own pay. Instead, the six-member Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation is responsible for setting legislator pay and benefits. The committee is made up of three appointees from the governor and three appointees from the Idaho Supreme Court. None of the committee members may hold a public office that is compensated with pay, according to the Idaho Constitution.
The Idaho Legislature is not in session, but will be soon.
The 2027 legislative session begins Jan. 11 at the Idaho State Capitol. Before that, the Idaho Legislature will convene for the organizational session in early December.
    Idaho legislators pay is set to go up, while state employees have gone without a raise
Since 2024, the pay raises given to state legislators have been significantly larger than the raises for regular state employees, which are set by the Idaho Legislature.
In 2024, the last time state legislators received a pay increase, the Citizens Committee on Legislative Compensation approved a 25% increase in legislative pay, from $19,913 a year to $25,000 per year.

title: Idaho health providers find successes, express frustration in year 1 of federal rural health grant
summary: After Idaho health officials had to “sprint” to award all of its nearly $186 million federal rural health care grants, a number of small health providers say they were left without answers about why their applications were denied. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron met with state legislators on the Rural Health […]
text:
Idaho health providers find successes, express frustration in year 1 of federal rural health grant
Some smaller hospital, clinic leaders say they worry their projects weren’t funded because they don’t have grant writers
Idaho has obligated its nearly $186 million federal Rural Health Transformation grant funds in the first year of the five-year program. Hospitals leaders who got awards say they'll make a big difference. Some smaller facilities who didn't get any funds say navigating the program was difficult without dedicated staff. (Getty Images)
After Idaho health officials had to “sprint” to award all of its nearly $186 million federal rural health care grants, a number of small health providers say they were left without answers about why their applications were denied.
Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron met with state legislators on the Rural Health Transformation Committee and healthcare providers and stakeholders on the Rural Health Transformation Program Implementation Task Force in two separate meetings on Thursday in Boise.
The Rural Health Transformation Program was created through the $50 billion Congress approved in July 2025 through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which also reduced an estimated nearly $1 trillion over 10 years in Medicaid spending nationwide. Idaho received about $186 million in the first year, and federal authorities announced on Nov. 9 the Gem State would receive nearly $183 million in year two.
Charron said staff are trying to determine why the state received less in the second year.
More than $103.5 million of Idaho’s grants in the first year were awarded to hospitals and clinics for infrastructure projects, equipment and technology upgrades in rural hospitals.
“The (electronic health record software), this is transformative for us. This is something that for us to do on our own, would take almost all our cash on reserves,” said Brad Turpen, CEO, Valor Health.
Valor Health, in Emmett, received two awards, totaling more than $5.4 million for a new electronic health record system that will connect to larger hospitals in the area, and new imaging equipment.
John Hennessy, CEO, Bonner General, said his hospital will be able to expand its surgical capacity by adding four new suites. The 25-bed hospital is the only hospital in the county, he said, and its operating room was at full capacity.
“A lot of our patients either have to wait long extended periods of time to get their surgeries done, or they end up traveling outside the area to get those procedures,” he said.
He said the volume of surgeries is expected to increase 23% in the first year with the new space that will be added.

Several small hospital and clinic leaders who didn’t get grants said their questions to the department about grants didn’t get answered, and they still are not sure why their application scored lower than others.

title: Nearly 40% of new Idaho inmates had drug charges, state watchdog report on overcrowded prisons finds
summary: In Idaho, which imprisons women at the highest rate in the nation, drug charges account for much of the state’s prison population, a new watchdog report found. The report by the independent state agency, the Office of Performance Evaluations, highlighted why the state has the seventh-highest incarceration rate in the nation, and the highest in […]
text:
Nearly 40% of new Idaho inmates had drug charges, state watchdog report on overcrowded prisons finds
Idaho has nation’s highest incarceration rate for women. Many are in custody on drug charges, new Office of Performance Evaluations report finds.
There are approximately 8,000 incarcerated individuals in nine state-owned prisons and five community reentry centers across Idaho. (Photo by Mia Maldonado/Idaho Capital Sun)
In Idaho, which imprisons women at the highest rate in the nation, drug charges account for much of the state’s prison population, a new watchdog report found.
The report by the independent state agency, the Office of Performance Evaluations, highlighted why the state has the seventh-highest incarceration rate in the nation, and the highest in the Mountain West. Over the past decade, drug possession sentences account for 39% of the state’s prison growth, more than any other crime, the agency’s researchers found.
Researchers said the drug crime data they analyzed didn’t show which drugs people were charged with being in possession of, or of trafficking. But user data they obtained from the state’s drug court system found that methamphetamine was by far the most reported, by 48% of people, with heroin and other opioids in second with 20%.
“While women are less likely than men to be incarcerated for drug possession, they are much less likely to be incarcerated for other crimes,” the report found. “More than half of the growth of women in custody over the past two decades comes from women convicted of a single drug possession charge.”
The 88-page report delivered a slew of statistics, including:
- Twice as many women were imprisoned in Idaho in 2025 than in 2005.
- Women are likely in prison for drug possession, even more than other drug offenses. Over a fifth, 22%, of females in prison in Idaho had just one drug possession sentence, compared to just 10% of males in prison.
- Nearly two thirds, 61%, of women in prisons had drug possession sentences, compared to 35% of men in prisons.
- Drug possession was the least likely category of crimes to have charges amended, with just 6% of felony cases being reduced to misdemeanors or lesser charges. Researchers used 2022 data for that metric to give court cases time to close. Researchers say that statistic can be explained by drug possession laws offering less sentencing options than other crimes, and inconsistencies in access to misdemeanor probation.
As the rest of the nation’s imprisonment rates fell amid declining crime rates, Idaho’s largely didn’t budge, the report found. The state kept incarcerating a similar share of people, even during years of peak population growth and reduced crime rates.
A bipartisan group of state lawmakers requested the study in March to help address the state’s overflowing prisons.
Four of the state’s largest counties — Ada, Canyon, Kootenai and Twin Falls — contributed the bulk, 87%, of growth in the state’s inmate population.

title: Boise Bench neighbors appeal city approvals for 5-cottage rental project on South Wilson Street
summary: Boise Bench neighbors appeal city approvals for 5-cottage rental project on South Wilson Street Idaho News 6
text:
BOISE BENCH, Idaho — Five rental cottages could soon be built on a half-acre lot here on South Wilson Street on the Boise Bench — but some neighbors are pushing back, appealing two city approvals that would help move the project forward.
WATCH: Boise Bench neighbors appeal approvals for 5-cottage rental project
As Boise grows, the city has been looking for ways to add more housing to existing neighborhoods, including smaller developments like cottage villages. The Wilson Cottage Court is one example.
Last week, Planning and Zoning approved a conditional use permit and variances for the property. That decision wasn't about whether five homes could go here. It was about some of the details — like where parking can go, how much landscaping is needed and how far the development has to sit from the property line.
The developer, Land Architect, said a 30-foot irrigation district easement takes up much of the north side of the property, limiting where the driveway and parking can go.
"We even tried to get more. Just so people can have storage, people have visitors, that sort of thing, so people don't have to park on the street. But the property has restrictions on it," property owner, Guy Skeele said.
The plan does exceed the city's parking requirements — one space per cottage. But neighbors said what works on paper doesn't necessarily work on this dead-end street.
"The code needs to be revisited,” neighbor Bob Johnson said.
Johnson, who lives in front of the property, said the project would fit better at a smaller scale.
"Five is too much. Take it down to three, we could live with it,” Johnson said.
Neighbors are also raising concerns about traffic as Wilson Street is a narrow one way street with a dead end.
"We have traffic turning around in our private driveways. It's part of living on a dead end, but usually dead ends are designed in a way that accommodates smaller amounts of residential traffic.” Katherine Barker, who lives across from the property, said.
They're also appealing a variance that would allow part of the landscape buffer to shrink from five feet to about three feet, eight inches.
And for the family next door, there's another concern. Right now, they cross part of the property to get to a building they use as a garage. At the hearing, the developer said there's no recorded easement giving them that access, and efforts to work out an agreement didn't pan out.
"We really like our little neighborhood back here.” Chris Scuglia said.
We're going to adapt. We're going to make some parking up front,” Erin Scuglia said.
The property owner said he's trying to add housing under the rules the city has put in place, while keeping these market-rate rentals as affordable as he can.
"The best policy is always to find a way to get along with them. Always be the best neighbor you can,” Skeele said.
Neighbors said they're not against more housing either — they just question how much fits here.

text:
Psychedelic mental healthcare for veterans wins bipartisan backing from US House panel
Nearly 6,500 veterans died by suicide in 2024, according to the latest Veterans Affairs Suicide Prevention Annual Report
The Department of Veterans Affairs in Washington, D.C., on June 22, 2026. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
NOTE: This story mentions suicide. If you or a loved one needs help during a mental health crisis, call or text 988, or visit 988helpline.org. Help is available for veterans and nonveterans alike.
WASHINGTON — Federal regulators could be on the cusp of approving psychedelic-assisted mental health treatment for veterans, but lawmakers asked tough questions Wednesday of Trump administration officials over whether the Department of Veterans Affairs can meet patients’ needs, and if federal law enforcement and health agencies are on the same page.
Just over 2 million veterans suffer with treatment-resistant depression, and approximately 180,000 of them would likely meet the criteria for treatment with psychedelic compounds, including MDMA, psilocybin, LSD, DMT and ibogaine, according to the Veterans Health Administration.
Members of the House Committee on Veterans Affairs Subcommittee on Health grilled officials for roughly two and a half hours during an afternoon hearing contemplating how the VA should implement the labor-intensive treatments if given the green light by the Food and Drug Administration.
Nearly 6,500 veterans died by suicide in 2024, according to the latest Veterans Affairs Suicide Prevention Annual Report, published in September.
“Something needs to change,” said subcommittee chair Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, R-Iowa, who said despite prevention efforts, the numbers have remained “stubbornly stagnant.”
“When I came to Congress in 2021, I didn’t think I’d be sitting here today advocating for these emerging breakthrough therapies, but in meeting with veterans from all walks of life, I have found the effectiveness of these treatments and am willing to advance it as potential hope,” said Miller-Meeks, who recently lost her bid for reelection.
Miller-Meeks, an Army veteran and ophthalmologist, cited randomized clinical trials for MDMA-assisted therapies that commenced this year at VA facilities in Rhode Island and Connecticut, both of which resulted from funding allocated in 2024.
Miller-Meeks also praised President Donald Trump’s April executive order directing the FDA to work with other agencies, including the VA, the Drug Enforcement Administration, and the Department of Health and Human Services to remove barriers, like drug enforcement classification, that complicate testing the treatments.
The possibility of new treatments was met with optimism on both sides of the aisle.
The subcommittee’s ranking member Rep. Julia Brownley, D-Calif., said the clinical trials are “extremely welcome news and will change lives for the better.”

New bird flu cases appear in dairy herds as state ag, vet officials seek vaccine urgency
Colorado, Idaho, Texas and Washington state have also reported cases of the virus among cattle over the past month
Cows from a non-suspect herd are seen at the Cornell Teaching Dairy Barn at Cornell University in 2024 in Ithaca, N.Y. States are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows. (Photo by Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images)
More states are seeing new cases of bird flu in cattle as state agricultural officials urge the federal government to prioritize approving vaccines for dairy cows.
The virus, highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, known commonly as bird flu, has been affecting poultry flocks for years. But in 2024, it was first detected in cows. Epidemiologists think cows initially contracted it via wild birds, and that the virus continued to spread between cattle via equipment and interstate transporting of asymptomatic dairy cattle.
While cases peaked in 2024, states are still seeing new infections in cattle this year. The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service reported that there are cases in states this year that previously hadn’t seen infections among dairy herds: Last Saturday, Oklahoma saw its first case since the outbreaks among cows began that year, according to data from the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Oregon also detected its first diagnosis at a dairy herd last week, as did Indiana, earlier this month, bringing the total number of states where the virus has been detected in dairy cattle to 22.
Colorado, Idaho, Texas and Washington state have also reported cases among cattle over the past month.
This year so far, there have been at least 146 dairy cattle infected with the virus, with more than 1,200 cases among cattle since the outbreak began.
On Nov. 6, the National Association of State Departments of Agriculture, which represents agricultural officials across all 50 states, and the National Assembly of State Animal Health Officials, wrote a letter to the USDA urging the agency to prioritize developing an emergency vaccination framework for cows, “to take additional action to control and ultimately eradicate” the virus in dairy cattle. Cattle can develop short-lived immunity to the virus but can get re-infected, the groups wrote.
The USDA says it supports rapid development and timely approval of a vaccine for dairy cattle, and several are undergoing field trials or awaiting final approval for emergency use. Developing and approving a vaccine has its own regulatory structure, and that can make for slow testing and implementation.
